title: Evaluating Urban Heat @ Tufts
text:
Students taking part in the Tufts Climate Resilience Institute summer program collected data on 27 July 2026 to evaluate relationships between surface temperatures, surface permeability, shade, and tree density on the Tufts Medford Campus.



CRI 2026 students collecting data (Credit: K Davies)




During the exercise, walked transects across the campus, stopping at intervals of 30 paces. At each observation point, the following data were recorded:

Surface temperature in degrees Celsius (taken using an infrared thermometer)
Surface type: impervious (dark/light) vs permeable (vegetated/unvegetated)
Shade level: complete, partial, or no shade
Tree density: number of trees in a 10 foot (3m) radius




CRI 2026 students collecting data (Credit: K Davies)





Data collection commenced at approximately 11AM EST in full sun conditions. students were positioned facing north or south at points along Professors’ Row, either side of Latin Way. The observations listed above, along with time and location, were collected using the ESRI Survey123 mobile application.



CRI 2026 students collecting data (Credit: K Davies)


A total of 306 observations were made during the exercise (see zoomable map below). The raw data can be accessed here.

Temperatures by surface type
Impervious surfaces store heat more effectively than permeable surfaces, and may continue radiating heat long after sundown. The boxplot below shows temperature ranges for data recorded on campus from different surfaces.

ggplot(dataClean,aes(x=`Surface type`,y=`Surface temperature`,fill=`Surface type`)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(y="Surface temperature (°C)") +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("darkred","indianred","beige","lightblue")) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

title: Evaluating Urban Heat @ Tufts
section: Temperature by surface type and shade
text:
Temperature by surface type and shade
This graph combines the three variables above (surface temperature, type, and shade). While the trends above still hold true, it demonstrates a more complex interplay between these factors. The cooling influence of surface permeability, for example, appears more significant in unshaded areas. The variation in temperatures is generally greater in areas of partial shade across all permeability categories. Temperatures are lower and much less variable in areas of complete shade. A few notable outliers of high temperature were recorded among the vegetated surfaces.

ggplot(dataClean,aes(x=`Surface type`,y=`Surface temperature`,fill=Shade)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_classic() +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("darkred","beige","lightblue")) +
  labs(y="Surface temperature (°C)")

text:
Data visualizations

Temperatures by surface type
Impervious surfaces store heat more effectively than permeable surfaces, and may continue radiating heat long after sundown. The boxplot below shows temperature ranges for data recorded on campus from different surfaces.











Temperature by shade
Trees intercept solar radiation that contributes to surface heating. The boxplot below shows temperature ranges for data recorded on campus from different shade categories.











Temperature by surface type and shade
This graph combines the three variables above (surface temperature, type, and shade). While the trends above still hold true, it demonstrates a more complex interplay between these factors. The cooling influence of surface permeability, for example, appears more significant in unshaded areas. The variation in temperatures is generally greater in areas of partial shade across all permeability categories. Temperatures are lower and much less variable in areas of complete shade. A few notable outliers of high temperature were recorded among the vegetated surfaces.











Temperature by tree density
Finally, we can examine how temepratures vary with respect to local tree density (expressed as number of trees within a 10 ft/3 m radius). This demonstrates a trend of cooler surface temperatures with greater tree density, though there is substantial variability across these values.

title: Code
text: R code to generate the visualizations in this website can be found below.

title: Code
section: Loading packages, data, and data cleaning
text:
Loading packages, data, and data cleaning

library(tidyverse)
library(terra)
library(tidyterra)
library(maptiles)
library(sf)
library(leaflet)

#read data
data<-read_csv("survey_0.csv")

#change default grass/bare earth labels to permeable (veg)/permeable (unveg), turn surface type and shade into factors 
dataClean<- data %>% 
 mutate(`Surface type`=replace_values(
   `Surface type`,
    "Turf grass"~"Permeable (vegetated)",
    "Bare earth"~"Permeable (unvegetated)")) %>%
  mutate(`Surface type`=factor(`Surface type`,levels=c("Impervious (dark-colored)","Impervious (light-colored)","Permeable (unvegetated)","Permeable (vegetated)"))) %>%
  mutate(Shade=factor(Shade,levels=c("No shade","Partial shade","Complete shade")))

title: Code
text:
Zoomable map

#convert data to spatial form
dataSpat<-dataClean %>%
  st_as_sf(coords=c("x","y"),crs=4326)

#make zoomable map with leaflet
leaflet(dataSpat) %>% 
  addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB) %>%
  addCircleMarkers(radius=0.5,color="black")

title: Code
text:
Mapping the data

Surface temperature

#get basemap
base<-get_tiles(dataSpat,provider="CartoDB.Positron")

#map surface temp
ggplot(dataSpat,aes(color=`Surface temperature`)) +
  geom_spatraster_rgb(data=base) +
  geom_sf() +
  scale_color_continuous(palette = c("lightblue", "#FC9272", "darkred")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(color="Surface temperature (°C)")










Surface type

#map surface type
ggplot(dataSpat,aes(color=`Surface type`)) +
  geom_spatraster_rgb(data=base) +
  geom_sf() +
  scale_color_manual(values=c("darkgrey","beige","tan","lightgreen")) +
  theme_minimal() 










Shade

#map shade
ggplot(dataSpat,aes(color=`Shade`)) +
  geom_spatraster_rgb(data=base) +
  geom_sf(alpha=0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values=c("lightblue","blue","darkblue")) +
  theme_minimal() 










Tree density

#create categorical value from tree density
dataSpat2<-dataSpat %>%
  mutate(densityCat=case_when(
    `Tree density`== 0 ~"No trees",
    `Tree density` %in% c(1.0,1.5,2.0) ~ "Low Density (1-2)",
    `Tree density` > 2 ~ "High Density (>2)"
  )) %>%
  mutate(densityCat,factor(densityCat,levels=c("No trees","Low Density (1-2)","High Density (>2)")))

#map tree density
base<-get_tiles(dataSpat,provider="CartoDB.Positron")
ggplot(dataSpat2,aes(color=densityCat)) +
  geom_spatraster_rgb(data=base) +
  geom_sf() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("darkseagreen4", "darkseagreen2","wheat1" )) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(color="Trees in 3m \nradius")
